name: Sacsayhuamán
label: Sacsayhuamán
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cristo Blanco' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cristo Blanco' (node/4746310711): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/83130621: large area 'Sacsayhuamán' (1454 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Inca fortress with huge zigzag stone walls above the city.

text.description:
Sacsayhuamán is the Inca citadel on the northern edge of Cusco, built on a steep hill above the city at about 3,701 metres. Chroniclers recorded that it was begun in the reign of Pachacuti and carried on by his successors. Its dry stone walls use huge blocks cut to fit tightly together without mortar, and that precision is what you want to capture. The walls are laid out in a zigzag above an open esplanade, with Cusco's rooftops and hills behind. Cusco and Sacsayhuamán were listed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

It is a companion shot to the walls rather than a close-up of them. From here you get a broad panorama of Cusco and its valley, with the statue as a foreground element. The walls are only a short walk away to the north-west and appear as a distant feature, not the main subject. Guides also suggest the lookout at Cruzmoqo, with its giant cross, for another wide city view. Confirm that one on the ground.

For close shots of the walls, walk across to the site itself. Stand back on the esplanade so the zigzag fills the frame, then step in close for the joints between the stones. Entry to the archaeological site needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Sacsayhuamán sits on the northern outskirts of Cusco, on a steep hill overlooking the historic city. The Cristo Blanco viewpoint is on the hilltop close by, to the south-east of the walls.
text.directions_text: No stations, tram stops or public transport are listed for this spot, so start from Cusco's historic centre and head up to the northern hillside. Ask for Cristo Blanco. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full valley panorama with the statue close in the foreground. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the city. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the distant walls to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Cristo Blanco (the hilltop viewpoint beside the statue). A broad panorama of Cusco and its valley, with the white statue as a foreground element; the Sacsayhuamán walls are only a short walk away rather than the main subject. Turn north-west for the walls, which are a short walk away and only a distant feature from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the statue on one third of the frame and let the city and valley fill the rest. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level. Try one wide shot and one zoomed shot toward the walls for contrast. If you also walk over to the site, the esplanade gives a view of the zigzag walls rising above the open ground. Cruzmoqo, with its giant cross, is an alternative lookout for a city view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the city to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour at sunset. Panorama mode works well for the valley if you move slowly and keep the phone level. Night mode may help once the light drops.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, according to guides. Arrive a little early to find a spot and try different framings.

text.access_note: The Sacsayhuamán archaeological site needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go; the Cristo Blanco viewpoint is listed as a free viewpoint.
claims_not_in_sources: Cold and high altitude can drain a phone battery faster than usual.
Panorama mode and night mode are usable at the Cristo Blanco viewpoint, depending on the phone and the light.

name: Coricancha
label: Qorikancha
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida El Sol' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Avenida El Sol nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/803941090: the OpenStreetMap point 'Qurikancha'.
notes: Inca sun temple with the Santo Domingo church built on top.

text.description: Coricancha was the most important temple of the Inca Empire, and its name in Quechua means 'golden temple'. Its walls were once covered in sheets of gold. After the Spanish conquest the temple was largely taken apart, and its stonework became the foundation of the Church and Convent of Santo Domingo, built in the 17th century after the 1650 earthquake. That mix of dark, rounded Inca masonry with a colonial church and convent beside it is what makes the place so rewarding to photograph. The Inca stone has stayed standing through major earthquakes that damaged the church above it, and the tightly fitted blocks show well in a close photo. You don't need to go inside for a good shot. From the pavement of Avenida El Sol you can see the curved temple wall with the church and convent alongside it, so it works as a quick outdoor stop. If you do go in, the garden and cloisters give a second view, with the rounded Inca wall set against the colonial arches. Photography is generally allowed inside, but not of the Cusco School paintings. Keep your phone steady against your body when you shoot, and stay aware of other people on the pavement while you frame the wall.
text.geographic_location: Coricancha is in Cusco, with the Santo Domingo church and convent built on top of the old temple. The street view is from Avenida El Sol, along the temple's outer wall.
text.directions_text: Walk to Avenida El Sol and look for Coricancha, or Qorikancha. Stop on the pavement facing the temple's street side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the curved Inca wall and the church and convent behind it. If the pavement is narrow and you can't step back, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for close shots of the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenida El Sol (facing the temple's street facade, from the sidewalk). The dark, rounded Inca temple wall seen from the street, with the colonial church and convent alongside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the curve of the wall along one of the lower lines, with the church rising above it. Keep the camera level so the straight lines of the building don't lean. For a second view, the garden inside the site shows the rounded Inca wall against the colonial arches and cloisters. Check the official site before you go to plan a visit inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and detail. Use the telephoto for details of the masonry, and hold the phone with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to the stonework than harsh midday sun. Go earlier or later if you want fewer people and less traffic in the frame.

text.access_note: The view from Avenida El Sol is from a public street, but the temple and convent inside are a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for current prices and opening hours.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually better for stone walls than harsh midday sun.
The pavement along Avenida El Sol can be narrow and busy with passers-by and traffic.
Avenida El Sol is a public street and the view from it is free.

name: Cusco Cathedral
label: Cusco Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Armas' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Armas' (node/6266294785): point; moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/448924553: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cuzco Cathedral' (133 m across).
notes: Colonial cathedral on the north side of the Plaza de Armas.

text.description:
Cusco Cathedral stands on the north-east side of the Plaza de Armas, and it is the most important religious monument in the historic centre. Its stone front is plain and heavy rather than fancy, and the two towers look short and sturdy. That is because the upper parts of the design were changed after the 1650 earthquake. The result is a calm, solid shape that fills a phone frame well, with the open plaza giving you room to step back.

The building has a layered history. The Spanish built it between 1560 and 1664 on the site of an Inca palace, the Kiswarkancha of the ruler Viracocha. Some of the red granite blocks were reused from the fortress of Sacsayhuamán. The cathedral complex covers about 3,920 square metres, and the historic centre of Cusco has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

For photographs, the best-known frame is straight in front of the cathedral, looking across the plaza and its gardens. You get the whole facade, the towers and the gardens in one picture. Early morning is the quietest time, and the light is softer then. After dark the facades are lit, which gives a very different mood. If you want a calmer view, Plaza Tricentenario shows the cathedral and the square with a fountain in the foreground. Mirador de San Cristóbal gives a distant view over the rooftops, but the climb can be tiring at Cusco's altitude.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Cusco, on the north-east side of the Plaza de Armas. The Church of the Triunfo is part of the same complex.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed near here. The Plaza de Armas is in the historic centre of Cusco, and the cathedral is on the north-east side of the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade across the plaza. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if people or trees crowd the edges and you want more of the gardens in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the towers, doorways and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Armas (in front of the Cathedral, facing the plaza and gardens). The cathedral's main facade framed across the open plaza and its gardens, the classic postcard angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep the phone level and use the gardens as a foreground. If you have time, Plaza Tricentenario is a calmer alternative with a fountain reflection, and Mirador de San Cristóbal gives a distant view of the cathedral with the Compañía church and the hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright part of the sky or the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone and sky keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 7 a.m., for soft light and few people, or after dark when the facades are lit.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working church, so the interior and some outside areas may have restrictions; check the official site before you go. The plaza in front is open public space.

name: Mercado Central de San Pedro
label: San Pedro Market
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OSM W66325451 (San Pedro Market): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Lively central market with food stalls and produce.

text.description:
Mercado Central de San Pedro is Cusco's central market, and it is a good place to photograph everyday life rather than monuments. Expect colour at close range: typical market goods, everyday scenes, and people serving, chatting and carrying goods. Because it is a working market, the best pictures are usually small scenes. Try a tidy pyramid of produce, a row of hanging items, or the light coming through the entrance into a busy aisle.

On the map the phone icon on the map sits on the market itself, so you take your photos from inside or at the entrance, with nothing to walk towards. The aisles can be narrow and crowded, so keep your elbows in, keep your phone close to your body when you are not shooting, and step aside so you do not block anyone who is working.

Start with the default lens (1x) for natural-looking shots of stalls. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when an aisle is too tight to fit a whole scene in. Use zoom (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details from a polite distance. Always ask before taking a close portrait of a stallholder; a smile and a gesture towards your phone usually works, and buying something small is a friendly way to start a conversation. I can't give you history or size figures for the market here, so look at the official local information if you want those.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot; use the map to reach the market. The phone icon on the map is the market itself, so you are in position as soon as you arrive. If you are already in the centre and fancy a walk, check the map for the walking route. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for narrow aisles and the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as produce and textiles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick a spot at the edge of an aisle or just inside an entrance, out of the way of customers and stallholders.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and look for a stall in the foreground, with the aisle leading back behind it. Fill the frame with colour: a pile of fruit, a row of bags or a flower stall. For people, use portrait mode only after asking permission.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest colour to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so bright patches at the entrance do not wash out. If the interior is dim, hold the phone steady against your body or a pillar and let night mode work if it switches on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is usually the liveliest, with the most stalls set up and the most activity. Quieter periods make it easier to take photos without blocking people.

text.access_note: Open public market, but check the official site or local information for opening times and any photography rules before you go.

name: Twelve-angled stone
label: Twelve-angled stone
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cuesta de San Blas' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Cuesta de San Blas nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1046924556: the OpenStreetMap point 'Twelve-angled-stone'.
notes: Famous Inca stone in the wall on Hatunrumiyoc street.

text.description:
The twelve-angled stone is a single block of green diorite set into the lower part of an old Inca wall. The wall once belonged to an Inca palace. Today it forms the outer side of the Archbishop's Palace, a colonial building that rises above it. The stone's edges have twelve corners, and its neighbours are cut to lock tightly around it. That fit is the reason people come.

It photographs well because the story is all in one frame. You get the pale, precisely cut Inca stonework below and the later colonial wall above, along a narrow pedestrian street. The stone is not huge, so a close-up of it alone can look flat. A wider view that includes the lane and the layers of wall tells you more about the place.

From there the wall is seen at an angle as you reach the bottom of the slope, with the lane leading into the picture. Expect crowds, handicraft sellers and a costumed 'Inca' who may ask for tips, so allow a little patience for a clear frame. Photography is allowed, but please do not touch or lean on the stones. Take your shot, then step back so others can see.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Cusco, on the pedestrian street of Hatun Rumiyoc, set into the outer wall of the Archbishop's Palace. The Cuesta de San Blas slope comes down to it from the San Blas side.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near here, so head to the Plaza de Armas area and continue on foot. From the Plaza de Armas, the usual way is up the Triunfo slope. The stone is to the south-west of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wall and the lane. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is busy and you cannot step back. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the stone from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Cuesta de San Blas (Coming down the slope toward the centre, so the wall is seen at an angle as you reach the bottom). The Inca wall and the stone approached from the San Blas side, with the narrow lane leading into the frame and a less crowded, more layered street scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Let the lane run diagonally into the picture and keep the stone in the lower third, with the colonial wall above it for context. Turn on gridlines and keep the wall's vertical lines straight, since the ultra-wide lens can bend them if you tilt the phone. For a close-up, tap on the stone's edges to focus. If you want a second angle, go to Hatun Rumiyoc and face the wall straight on, so the twelve-angled block and its interlocking neighbours fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stonework keeps its texture and the sky does not turn white. Take a few frames, because people often walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try going early in the day, when the lane is likely to be quieter. Check how the sun falls on the wall when you arrive.

text.access_note: The stone is on an open pedestrian street where photography is allowed but touching is not; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit the Archbishop's Palace itself.

name: Church of San Blas
label: San Blas Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plazoleta de San Blas' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plazoleta de San Blas' (way/86684420): middle (75 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/68629618: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'San Francisco de Asís' (82 m across).
notes: Small church in the artisan San Blas quarter, known for its carved pulpit.

text.description:
San Blas is a church on a small cobbled square at the foot of the San Blas slope, in the artisan quarter just above Cusco's historic centre. It is a good place for a relaxed, close-up photo. The church front sits on the square, and the narrow streets lined with craft workshops climb away on every side, so the surroundings help the picture instead of fighting it.

Once you are on the square, face the church front so you can get the facade, the cobbles and a slice of the lanes around it in one frame. Visitor guides describe this plaza as the place where the church stands and a good spot for photos. They also say the streets lead up to it from the historic centre, so you arrive on foot through the quarter's lanes.

The square is small, so use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the whole facade without stepping back into a doorway or a stall. Then switch to the default lens (1x) or a zoom (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for doors, stonework and street details.

If you want a wider view with the church as one landmark among many, the Mirador de San Blas looks over the red-tiled roofs of the centre. Photography is generally not allowed inside the church, so plan on exterior shots only.
text.geographic_location: In the San Blas neighbourhood on the hillside above Cusco's historic centre, on the small Plazoleta de San Blas at the foot of the San Blas slope.
text.directions_text: Start from the historic centre of Cusco and follow the artisan-lined streets uphill towards the San Blas slope; the streets lead up to the small square by the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the facade and the square into one frame, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. A 2x to 5x zoom, if your phone has one, suits doorway and stonework details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plazoleta de San Blas (in front of the church facade on the small square at the foot of the San Blas slope). The church's front on its small square, with the cobbled plaza and the artisan-lined streets around it in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the facade upright and the cobbles in the lower third. Include a street running off the square to give a sense of the quarter. For a wider view where the church is one landmark among many, try the Mirador de San Blas above the red-tiled roofs. Kiskapata Street on the slope gives side-on views of the church area.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Keep the phone level, because the square is tight and a tilted wide-angle shot will make the walls lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is a good bet for softer light and a quieter square; check how the light falls on the facade when you arrive.

text.access_note: The square is a public space, but the church is a place of worship where photography is generally not allowed inside, so check current access and any street works before you go.

San Blas is on a slope above, and uphill from, the historic centre of Cusco.

name: Inka Museum
label: Inka Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/965131815: the OpenStreetMap point 'Inca Museum'.
notes: Museum of Inca culture in a colonial mansion near the Plaza de Armas.

text.description: The Inka Museum is the archaeological museum of the National University of San Antonio Abad of Cusco, and it sits in the Casa del Almirante, a 17th-century colonial house on Cuesta del Almirante. For a phone photographer the building is the draw. Its old stonework and the street outside make a good record of a Cusco morning or afternoon. The house has a long story. The site was once the home of Huáscar in the Inca Empire. The house later passed to the archbishopric, then became the palace of the last viceroy, and then the Government House of Marshal Santa Cruz. The 1950 earthquake damaged it. The museum itself was founded in 1920 and today shows keros, textiles, mummies, tools, weapons and goldsmithing. Its displays follow the history of Cusco from its beginnings to the 20th century. Outside, start with the whole frontage, then move closer for details such as doorways, carved stone and the texture of the walls. Keep your phone level, or use the gridlines, so the walls don't lean. If you plan to go inside, check current visiting arrangements locally before you go. Photography rules for the displays can differ from those for the street outside.
text.geographic_location: The museum is on Cuesta del Almirante, in the city of Cusco, Peru. It occupies the colonial Casa del Almirante, also called the Admiral's Palace.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop serves this spot, so start from the centre of Cusco and walk or take a taxi to Cuesta del Almirante. Ask for the Inka Museum (Museo Inka) or the Casa del Almirante. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself, so once you reach the museum's frontage you are there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the frontage. If space is tight and the whole building won't fit in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for doorways, stone details and upper windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back along Cuesta del Almirante if you need more of the frontage in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the wall edges with the vertical lines so the building stands straight. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then a closer 2x shot of the doorway or stonework. If you tilt up with the ultra-wide, the walls will lean inwards, so step back where you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and texture. Wipe the lens before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go earlier or later in the day rather than at midday, when the light is flat and harsh.

text.access_note: The museum is run by the National University of San Antonio Abad of Cusco; check current visiting arrangements locally before you go. The street outside is public.

name: Plaza de Armas, Cusco
label: Plaza de Armas
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OSM N6266294785 (Plaza de Armas): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The main square of Cusco, framed by arcades, the cathedral and the Jesuit church.

text.description: The Plaza de Armas is the main square of Cusco and the natural starting point for a walk round the city centre. It is a broad open space, so it works well for photographs that show the whole scene as well as for small details: people crossing the square, the buildings around the edges, and the lamps and balconies that frame the view. Because the square is large, the best picture is usually taken from a little way back, not from the middle. The phone icon on the map is about 95 m east of the subject. From there you can look west across the open space and include the buildings on the far side, with some sky above them. Start with the default lens (1x) and turn on the gridlines so the horizon and the building edges stay straight. If the square is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or use people as part of the picture to give a sense of scale. If the sky is bright, tap on a darker part of the scene and lower the exposure slider a little to keep the sky from washing out. Take a few frames at different heights, standing and with the phone held lower, and keep the one with the cleanest foreground.
text.geographic_location: The Plaza de Armas is in the central, historic part of Cusco, at the heart of the old town.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Cusco and ask for the Plaza de Armas. Stand there and look west to see the square as the map shows it. The phone icon on the map is about 95 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the buildings and sky, and to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 95 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the buildings on the far side along one of the horizontal lines. Keep a little sky at the top and some open ground at the bottom. Use people crossing the square to add scale, and hold the phone level to avoid leaning walls with the ultra-wide lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something firm or brace the phone against your body to keep it still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, with fewer people in the square. Around dusk the lights come on and night mode can give a warm, even picture.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but access and events may vary, so be prepared for changes on the day.

The square is a large open space surrounded by buildings, with sky visible above them.
The square is an open public space that can be entered freely.

name: Church of the Society of Jesus, Cusco
label: La Compañía de Jesús
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23799161: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of the Society of Jesus' (94 m across).
notes: Baroque Jesuit church with a gilded altarpiece.

text.description: The Church of the Society of Jesus (Iglesia de la Compañía de Jesús) stands on Cusco's main square, the Plaza de Armas. It was built on the site of Amarucancha, an Inca palace that belonged to the ruler Huayna Capac. It is counted among the best examples of Spanish Baroque architecture in Peru. The first church was badly damaged in the 1650 earthquake. It was rebuilt and finished in 1673, and the Flemish Jesuit Jean-Baptiste Gilles is named as its architect. The whole church is built of pink basalt and andesite, so the stone has a warm colour that works well in a photo. The front is a symmetrical Baroque design with two projecting towers on either side of a carved central section. That balance makes it easy to frame on a phone. The building is large, about 94 m across, so you will need to choose between the whole front and a close-up of the carving. Take both if you have time: a wide shot to show the church beside the square, then a tighter shot of the stonework. Keep your phone upright and level so the towers don't lean. Wait a moment for people to cross the frame, as the square is a busy place.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Cusco, on the Plaza de Armas, close to the Cathedral.
text.directions_text: Head for the Plaza de Armas in the centre of Cusco. Once you are on the square, look for the twin towers and the pinkish stone front. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full front and both towers, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved central section.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Face south-east and keep the church in the middle of the screen.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the two towers up with the vertical lines so the building stands straight. Leave a little sky above the towers. Then step in or zoom to 2x-5x for a close shot of the carved stone and the window above the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone front to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the pink stone does not wash out. Hold the phone with both hands, as a steady grip helps in lower light.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually has fewer people on the square. Soft light in the morning or late afternoon suits the stone. After dark, try night mode if the front is lit, and brace your arms against something steady.

text.access_note: This is a working church and heritage site on a public square, so check the official site before you go for visiting rules, and dress modestly if you plan to go in.

name: Qenko
label: Qenko
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Q'enqo' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jirón Q'enqo' (way/4823910): point nearest the subject (158 m long).
notes: Inca ceremonial site carved into the rock.

text.description:
Q'enqo (also spelled Qenko, Kenko or Quenco) is a ceremonial site built around a great natural outcrop of rock, a little way out of Cusco and east of Sacsayhuamán. The name comes from the Quechua word for "zig-zag". It is counted among the largest huacas, or holy places, in the Cusco Region, and it is thought to have been used for sacrifices and mummification. Inside the rock a tunnel leads past a channel cut along one side to a small room with a ceremonial table and niches on either side. One niche is said to have held mummies, and another a large silver plate that threw sunlight into the room.

For photographs, the best-known spot is the semi-circular Amphitheater area inside the site. From there you can fit the carved monolith and the stone-walled curve together in one frame, with the valley behind. The mix of pale carved stone, steps and open sky gives the picture depth even on a phone. Walk around the rock before you settle on a view, because the carved surfaces change a lot as you move. A second option is the eucalyptus woodland nearby, which shows the ruins against the trees and gives a wider, more open view of the Cusco landscape. It is a less certain pick, so treat it as a bonus. Visit early or late in the day, when the light is softer and fewer people are around.
text.geographic_location: Q'enqo is in the Cusco District of Cusco Province, a few kilometres north-east of the city centre and just east of Sacsayhuamán.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or Underground-style stops to give you here. Start from the centre of Cusco and go north-east, towards Sacsayhuamán, with Q'enqo a little further east. If you are asking for directions, ask for Q'enqo (also written Qenko). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Amphitheater and the monolith together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole curve of the stonework and the valley in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the carved steps and the rock surface, or for a distant view of the site from where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (the semi-circular Amphitheater area of the site). The carved monolith and stone-walled amphitheater of the ruin, framed against the valley. From there the view is a distant one towards the north-west, not a close-up of the rock.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level. Inside the site, place the monolith on one of the vertical lines, with the valley filling the space behind it. From where you stand, frame the site to the north-west as a small element in the wider landscape. If you have time, the eucalyptus woodland nearby gives a second view, with the ruins set against the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the monolith to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail against the bright sky. Photography inside the underground chambers may be restricted, so check the signs on site before you take your phone out there.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the crowds are thinner.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed archaeological site covered by the Cusco tourist ticket, so check the official site before you go for current ticket rules and opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: Low-angle light makes the texture of carved stone stand out more on a phone photo.
Bright sky behind pale stone can fool a phone's automatic exposure.

text.description:
Santa Catalina Convent is in Cusco. The photo here shows the convent as seen from the small square beside it, the Plazoleta Santa Catalina. It works well on a phone because you can take it from an easy, short distance without needing a wide-open view.

Face that way and look for the convent from there. I have no dated history or measurements to quote for this place, so use the official site or a local guide if you want the story behind the building.

Start with the whole frontage, then move in for details that catch your eye, such as the stonework or any signs. Be aware of passers-by and take your time. Switch on the gridlines so the vertical lines of the building stay straight. If you cannot fit everything in, step back a little, or use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), and keep the phone level to avoid leaning walls. Inside the convent, photography rules may differ, so check before you take any pictures there.
text.geographic_location: In Cusco, at the Plazoleta Santa Catalina, the small square by the Santa Catalina Convent.
text.directions_text: The Plazoleta Santa Catalina, the small square by the convent, is about 39 metres to the south-east, less than a minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for the convent as you see it. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole building in. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Look for the convent from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the edge of the building up with a vertical line. Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then a closer one of a detail. Keep the phone upright and level so the walls do not lean. If people walk past, wait a moment and you may get a clear frame, or include them for a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little if the sky is washing out. If a part of the wall is in shade, tap there and lift the slider slightly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the walls and fewer harsh shadows. Midday sun can be strong and contrasty.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements for the convent itself, as access and photography rules inside may be restricted.

name: Church of San Francisco, Cusco
label: San Francisco Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza San Francisco' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza San Francisco' (way/24025873): middle (162 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/68629618: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'San Francisco de Asís' (82 m across).
notes: Colonial church and convent on Plaza San Francisco.

text.description:
The Church of San Francisco is a Franciscan church on the square that shares its name, in the historic centre of Cusco. It has a plainer look than many of the city's churches, which suits a photograph. The stone facade is in the Plateresque style, and a single tower with seven bells rises beside it. The simple lines and carved detail make a clean, calm picture, especially against the colonial buildings around the square.

The Franciscans moved to this site in 1549. The church was built from 1572 onwards, rebuilt in the 1640s, and finished again in 1652 after the 1650 earthquake. It sits next to the Franciscan convent, whose museum holds a very large 17th-century painting of the order's family tree. The church has been part of Cusco's historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, since 1983.

For your photo, stand on Plaza San Francisco, in front of the church. From here you get a straight-on view of the front of the building, with the square's colonial buildings framing it. The square is usually quieter than the Plaza de Armas, so you have more room to line up the shot. For a wider, more distant view, the Mirador de Santa Ana looks across the red-tiled rooftops, with the church dome visible; check its exact location on the map first. Inside, the carved cedarwood high choir (1652) is notable, but check what photography is allowed first.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Cusco, on Plaza San Francisco, about 300 metres southwest of the Plaza de Armas. The Franciscan convent and the Colegio Ciencias stand next to it.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are given for Cusco, so start from the Plaza de Armas. Head southwest to Plaza San Francisco, about 5 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight-on view of the facade and tower. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and the surrounding buildings in the frame. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved stonework and the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza San Francisco (in front of the church facade, on the square that shares the church's name). The church's front facade and carved stonework, framed by the colonial buildings that line the square. The church is to the west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the tower and the edges of the facade with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Include some of the square's old buildings on either side to frame the church. For a different view, try the Mirador de Santa Ana, which shows the church dome among the red-tiled rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Stone and sky are often very different in brightness. If you are close, hold the phone level to keep the facade straight. Panorama mode can capture the whole square, but move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the square. Check that the facade is lit rather than in shadow when you arrive.

text.access_note: The square outside is free to visit. Going inside the church is ticketed, so check the official site for the museum and crypts.

name: Museo de Arte Precolombino, Cusco
label: Pre-Columbian Art
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q4306262: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Museum of pre-Columbian art in the Casa Cabrera courtyard.

text.description:
The Museo de Arte Precolombino, often shortened to MAP, sits in a Colonial mansion on Plazoleta de las Nazarenas in Cusco's San Blas district. The building has a long history. It began as an Inca ceremonial courthouse, was acquired in 1580 by the conquistador Alonso Díaz, and was then built over in Colonial style as the home of the Viceroy Hernandez de Cabrera. After many changes of owner and use it fell into ruin. It was restored and re-opened as a museum in June 2003.

Inside, around 450 pieces are on permanent display, drawn from the Larco Museum in Lima. They cover the period from 1250 BC to AD 1532 and are arranged in ten galleries, including Nasca, Mochica, Inca, Jewelry and Stone, Silver, and Gold and Metals.

For photographers, the appeal is the setting: a historic stone building with Colonial character, in Cusco's San Blas district. If there is room, step back and show the building with its surroundings, so start there. Take one wide shot for context, then move closer for architectural details. Keep your phone upright for the entrance and turn it sideways to take in the width of the frontage. If you go inside, ask staff whether photography is allowed in the galleries before you take any pictures.
text.geographic_location: In Cusco's San Blas district, on Plazoleta de las Nazarenas.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops to give as a starting point. Head for the San Blas district and ask for Plazoleta de las Nazarenas. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so once you reach the plazoleta you are in the right place. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building as you see it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole frontage in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The map position of the building is approximate, so if there is room, step back to take it in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical edges of the building parallel to the grid lines so the walls don't lean. Take one wide shot with a little of the surroundings for context, then one or two close shots of the entrance or architectural details. Keep passers-by in the frame if you like, as they show the scale of the place.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building's wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and detail. If the ultra-wide lens stretches the edges, move back and use the default lens (1x) instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the walls. At midday the shadows are harder, so look for shaded details instead.

text.access_note: The museum is a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for opening arrangements, tickets and any photography rules inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and warmer than midday light.
Photography rules inside museum galleries vary, so staff may restrict it.
Tickets or entry rules may apply for visiting the museum.
There may be room on the plazoleta to step back from the building.

name: Colcampata
label: Colcampata
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza San Cristóbal' (5 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Mirador de San Cristobal' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5776671: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Inca terraces and wall above the city with a view over the centre.

text.description:
Colcampata is the old Inca palace foundations on the hillside above Cusco's historic centre, with the San Cristóbal church built on top. For a phone photo, the draw is the layering. Neat Inca walls fill the foreground, the church bell tower rises behind them, and the city rooftops stretch away beyond. It is a small square, so you can take your time over the framing.

The site is an archaeological site in the Cusco District and has been declared a National Cultural Heritage of Peru. The name comes from Quechua, and it points to an elevated place or edge, which suits the hillside setting.

The best-known photo comes from Plaza San Cristóbal, the small square in front of the church where the Inca walls stand. From there the walls, the bell tower and the rooftops all fit into one frame, and you also get a close view towards the Plaza de Armas. Be aware that some visitors find fences and wires get in the way of clean shots, so move a few steps along the square and try different angles until the walls are clear.

The climb is steep and cobbled, and the altitude is about 3,400 m, so go slowly and bring water. If you want a wider view afterwards, Mirador de Cristo Blanco looks over the Colcampata hillside and San Blas, with the historic centre and Huatanay valley beyond.
text.geographic_location: Colcampata is on the hillside above the San Blas neighbourhood in Cusco District, beneath the San Cristóbal church. It looks down over the historic centre.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops serve this spot. From the historic centre or the Plaza de Armas, go uphill towards San Blas and the San Cristóbal church. The last stretch is steep and cobbled, so allow extra time on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the walls, bell tower and rooftops sit together. Switch to telephoto (2x or more) to pick out stonework or crop out fences and wires. The ultra-wide (0.5x) can help if you are close to the walls, but keep the phone level so the lines do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza San Cristóbal (in front of the San Cristóbal church, where the Inca walls stand). The Inca walls of the Colcampata palace in the foreground, with the San Cristóbal church bell tower and the city rooftops beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the walls along the lower third, with the bell tower upright beside them. If a fence or wire crosses the view, shuffle sideways or hold the phone close to a gap. If you also visit Mirador de Cristo Blanco, use it for a wide shot of the hillside and the city instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Tapping on a wall rather than a wire helps the phone avoid focusing on the fence.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the recommended time for good light over the city, and one guide suggests sunrise. If the light is fading, steady the phone against a wall and let night mode do its work.

text.access_note: Plaza San Cristóbal is a free public square.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone close to a gap in a fence can help keep the fence out of the shot.
Tapping on a wall rather than a wire helps the phone focus on the wall.
Steadying the phone against a wall helps keep night shots sharp.
The route up from the historic centre is uphill (the hillside is above San Blas).
